Composition describes each species' share of the trees. Using the
[shared simulated forest](plot-sampling-data.html), we relate the allocation
of trees among pine, oak, and birch to canopy height. We fit a composition-only
model, compare its coefficients with their generating values, and estimate
forest-wide species proportions conditional on known total counts in the
prediction cells.

::: {.alert .alert-info role="note"}
**Example data**

[Download the plot-sampling data (ZIP)](downloads/plot-sampling.zip){.btn .btn-primary download="plot-sampling.zip"}

The introductory plot-sampling articles use this same archive.
Extract it and use the folder containing `data/` as your R working directory.
:::

## Read the data

We use the same 151 sampled plots and 4,812 prediction cells as the
[magnitude article](magnitude-plot-sampling.html). The tables contain
simulated total counts and species-by-DBH counts, along with plot or cell
area in hectares and standardized canopy height `x`. We read both tables
and sum the DBH-class counts within each species.

```{r}
#| label: read-data

library(magComp)
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(1)

plots <- read_csv("data/plots.csv")

prediction <- read_csv("data/prediction.csv")

species_order <- c("pine", "oak", "birch")

# Columns such as pine:10-20 contain species-by-DBH counts.
trees <- plots |>
  select(plot_id, area, x, contains(":")) |>
  pivot_longer(contains(":"), names_to = c("species", "dbh_class"),
               names_sep = ":", values_to = "count") |>
  group_by(plot_id, area, x, species) |>
  summarise(count = sum(count), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(species = factor(species, levels = species_order)) |>
  arrange(plot_id, species)

trees |>
  filter(plot_id == 1) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

The resulting `trees` table has one row per plot and species, including
species with zero counts. The predictor `x` is p95 standardized using the
plots' mean and standard deviation; the same scaling was applied to the
prediction cells in the data article.

## Model species composition

For plot $i$, let $N_i$ be its total tree count, $y_{ij}$ the count of
species $j$, and $p_{ij}$ that species' probability. The probabilities sum
to one, and the model allocates the known total using

$$
(y_{i1},y_{i2},y_{i3}) \mid N_i,\mathbf p_i
\sim \operatorname{Multinomial}(N_i,\mathbf p_i).
$$

We use the species sequence pine, oak, birch. The model first allocates trees
to pine, then allocates some of the remaining trees to oak; birch receives
the rest. Let $\pi_{i1}$ be the pine probability and $\pi_{i2}$ the oak
probability among trees that are not pine. The default probit link gives

$$
\pi_{ij}=\Phi(\alpha_{0j}+\alpha_{1j}x_i),\qquad j=1,2,
$$

where $\alpha_{0j}$ and $\alpha_{1j}$ are the intercept and slope for
allocation step $j$. The standard normal distribution function $\Phi$,
implemented by `pnorm()` in R, converts the linear expression to a
probability. The overall species probabilities are

$$
p_{i1}=\pi_{i1},\qquad
p_{i2}=(1-\pi_{i1})\pi_{i2},\qquad
p_{i3}=(1-\pi_{i1})(1-\pi_{i2}).
$$

For example, if pine receives 50% of the trees and oak receives 60% of those
remaining, the overall proportions are 50% pine, 30% oak, and 20% birch.
Birch has no separate coefficient row. Species have no natural order;
the chosen sequence defines the allocation steps and the interpretation of
their coefficients.

## Fit and examine parameter estimates

`magCompData()` obtains each plot's total by summing its species counts.
We set `magnitude = NULL` to fit composition alone. The formula `~ x`
supplies an intercept and canopy-height slope for each allocation step,
and `ordered = FALSE` specifies unordered species categories without
smoothing across them.

```{r}
#| label: fit

dat <- magCompData(
  trees,
  unit = plot_id, category = species, tree_count = count,
  ordered = FALSE, design = fixedArea(area)
)

fit <- magComp(
  dat,
  magnitude = NULL,
  composition = ~ x,
  control = magCompControl(
    n_samples = 2000,
    n_burn = 1000,
    n_chains = 3,
    n_cores = 3,
    chain_seeds = 1:3,
    verbose = FALSE
  )
)
```

We use default independent Normal coefficient priors and starting values.
Each of three MCMC chains runs for 2,000 iterations and discards the first
1,000, leaving 3,000 draws for parameter summaries. Plot area is not needed
to estimate species probabilities, but supplying it allows conditional
counts to be expressed as densities.

We compare the estimated coefficients with the values used in the data
article. Named values match each parameter's printed index.

```{r}
#| label: parameter-estimates

true_alpha <- c("pine:(Intercept)" = 0, "pine:x" = 0.5,
                "oak:(Intercept)" = -0.5, "oak:x" = -0.5)

parameter_summary <- summary(fit)
parameter_summary$truth <- true_alpha[parameter_summary$index]

parameter_summary |>
  select(symbol, truth, mean, q2_5, q97_5, rhat, ess) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    col.names = c("Parameter", "Truth", "Mean", "2.5%", "97.5%", "R-hat", "ESS")
  )
```

The labels `alpha[0,pine]` and `alpha[x,pine]` denote pine's intercept and
slope. Applying `pnorm()` to an intercept gives the conditional probability
at average plot p95. A positive slope increases that probability as canopy
height increases; for oak, this describes its share among trees remaining
after pine. The slopes are on the probit scale, so they are not constant
percentage-point changes in species proportions.

The mean and 2.5% and 97.5% columns give posterior estimates and 95% credible
intervals. All four generating values fall within these intervals.
R-hat values near one indicate agreement among chains; ESS is
the effective sample size after accounting for dependence among iterations.

## Predict forest composition

Species probabilities can be predicted from canopy height alone. To
estimate each species' share of all trees in the forest, we also need the
abundance in each cell. Here we supply the simulated cell totals as known
inputs using `total_count = "count"`. The cell's species counts remain
unknown to the model and are used below to calculate truth.

For each retained parameter draw, `target = "observation"` allocates each
cell's total among the species with a multinomial draw. We request density,
which divides the resulting species counts by cell area, and use 100 draws
per chain for prediction.

```{r}
#| label: predict

predictions <- predict(
  fit,
  prediction |> select(plot_id, x, area, count),
  total_count = "count",
  type = "density",
  target = "observation",
  n_draws = 100,
  summary = "samples"
)

# Prediction cell x species x retained draw x chain.
dim(predictions$density)
```

The array contains 4,812 cells, three species, 100 draws, and three chains.
Each allocation sums to its supplied cell total. Uncertainty comes from the
coefficients and species allocation, conditional on those fixed totals.

We pass these draws to `standSummary()` to calculate forest composition.
Within each draw, it multiplies species densities by represented cell areas,
sums over cells, and divides each species' total by the total across species.
Thus, cells with more trees contribute more to the forest's species proportions.
Omitting `group` produces one forest-wide summary.

```{r}
#| label: forest-composition

forest_predictions <- standSummary(
  predictions,
  data = prediction,
  unit = plot_id,
  represented_area = area,
  type = "proportion",
  summary = "samples"
)

forest_summary <- summary(forest_predictions)
forest_summary
```

The `mean` column gives each species' estimated share of forest trees.
The `q2_5` and `q97_5` columns bound its 95% posterior predictive interval.
Species proportions sum to one in every draw, as do their posterior means;
their separate interval endpoints need not sum to one.

## Compare with truth

We calculate true proportions by summing the simulated species-by-DBH
counts across prediction cells and DBH classes, then dividing each species'
total by the forest total. These are the same cell-area weights used above,
since multiplying a cell's density by its area returns its count.

```{r}
#| label: forest-truth

forest_truth <- prediction |>
  select(contains(":")) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("species", "dbh_class"),
               names_sep = ":", values_to = "count") |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(count = sum(count), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(truth = count / sum(count))

comparison <- forest_summary |>
  as_tibble() |>
  rename(species = category) |>
  left_join(forest_truth, by = "species") |>
  mutate(species = factor(species, levels = species_order))
```

We show the estimated proportions and their intervals alongside the known
forest proportions.

```{r}
#| label: fig-forest-composition
#| fig-cap: "Forest species proportions. Blue points and bars show posterior means and 95% posterior predictive intervals conditional on known cell totals. Black horizontal marks show simulated truth."

ggplot(comparison, aes(species, mean)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = q2_5, ymax = q97_5), width = 0.12,
                color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2", size = 3) +
  geom_point(aes(y = truth), shape = 95, size = 8) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of forest trees") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The estimates closely match the known forest composition, and all three
true proportions fall within their intervals. These intervals condition on
known cell totals. When those totals must also be estimated, we combine
magnitude and composition to predict both abundance and its allocation.
The next article does this for [DBH classes across all species](dbh-plot-sampling.html),
followed by a [species-by-DBH model](full-model-plot-sampling.html).
Both carry uncertainty from magnitude and composition into forest and stand
summaries.
